messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 41‑year‑old South Asian park ranger, returned from a covert military deployment where he had been held captive for three months in a remote compound. He tells the story in short, hard‑cut images: the weight of the chain around his wrist, the smell of gunpowder that lingered long after the walls collapsed, and the sharp sting of his own blood as he was dragged to the edge of a canyon. In the quiet moments after the raid, he could hear the echo of gunfire as if it were a drumbeat, and the memory of that night crystallized into a series of snapshots that he could replay in his mind with unsettling clarity. Those images carry the same physical pain he feels in his shoulders whenever they come back. Back in the parks, everyday conversations about the Army’s newest equipment and the tactical drills his coworkers rehearse trigger a flood of those snapshots. The moment a colleague mentions a new rifle, Arjun’s eyes widen; the memory of being held at gunpoint replays, and the startle response flares as he scrambles to find cover behind a fallen log. The trigger of “being seen” in the open trail, a uniformed patrol car driving past, or any mention of military strategy makes him feel as though the past is intruding into the present. Those triggers are the catalysts that pull the memory into focus and simultaneously reinforce his sense of isolation, humiliation, and the belief that anyone else would never have had to endure such a nightmare. This chain of feeling pushes him toward maladaptive strategies: he begins to restrict his food intake to a tight schedule of two small meals, a ritual that offers a strange sense of control. He also starts rehearsing revenge fantasies, imagining a future where he can finally make the captors pay, and he goes along with every plan his coworkers propose in order to keep the peace, people‑pleasing to stave off any confrontation that might remind him of his humiliation. When the memory returns, it is not only the flashbacks that attack him; the threat that accompanies them is equally brutal. He finds himself hyper‑vigilant, unable to trust even his own sense of safety. A sudden breeze that rustles the leaves on a lonely trail becomes a perceived assault, and he reacts as though a knife might strike him. This threat, in turn, pulls him deeper into the memory, tightening the loop of fear. The physical pain he feels in his chest when the memory surfaces reminds him of the day he was shackled to a tree, making the threat more tangible and the memory more vivid. The negative appraisals—his feeling of being humiliated and set apart—reinforce the memory and feed back into the triggers. As he avoids discussions about military topics, he inadvertently heightens his sensitivity to them, because the avoidance keeps the mind on high alert for a perceived threat. The same avoidance makes him less likely to report a safety concern on the trail, increasing his fear that he will again be put in a vulnerable position. When he restricts his eating, the physical weakness he experiences feels like a failure, confirming the belief that he is less capable than others, which again solidifies his isolation and humiliation. Each of these strategies, each of these thoughts, each of these triggers loops back to feed the memory and the threat, creating a self‑reinforcing cycle that has taken hold over the past nine months. The cumulative effect has been an erosion of his professional confidence. A routine inventory of supplies now takes him longer because he is preoccupied with whether the act of eating might feel like a betrayal of his strict diet, and he avoids the briefing room whenever a senior ranger in uniform speaks, fearing the echo of authority. In his personal life, he has begun to postpone visits to his partner, insisting she keep busy, because any intimate conversation feels like a potential trigger. The guilt of not being able to share his fears adds to his sense of isolation. In therapy, he described how he had stopped telling his partner about the night he was held captive because it would make her uncomfortable, a form of people‑pleasing that protects him from the humiliation he feels every time he thinks of the event. Arjun’s decision to seek help came after a particularly severe flashback that occurred while he was alone in the ranger station’s storage area, a space he had always considered safe. He was unable to breathe, his heart hammered, and he felt a phantom sense of being held at gunpoint again, as if a threat had manifested in the dim light of the locker room. The next morning, he realized that he could no longer function, even in the most routine tasks. He fears that his memories will erupt at any moment, that his partner might lose faith in him, and he hopes that therapy will give him a way to reclaim control and diminish the terror that still grips his life.
